title: Helping an adult with their medicines
intro: If someone you care about is starting or continuing gender-affirming hormone therapy, you can make a real difference. This page explains what the medicines are. It covers the everyday problems that can come up at the pharmacy. It also shows how to help without taking over.

body: Gender-affirming hormone therapy uses common medicines that have been used for a long time. They include oestrogen and testosterone, in the same forms used for menopause and low hormone levels. Other medicines lower or block hormones the person does not want. GPs and specialists prescribe them under Australian standards of care. Any pharmacy can fill the script. The [Medicines A–Z](#/medicines) has a plain-language page on each one. The [Easy Read guides](#/easy) say the same things in fewer words.

Day to day, the problems are rarely medical. A patch brand may be out of stock. A script may have expired. A pharmacy may quote a private price when the PBS price applies. Or the name on a label may be wrong. The [supply page](#/supply), the [costs guide](#/costs) and the [pharmacy guide](#/pharmacy) are made for these moments. You can use them on someone's behalf.

Serious problems are uncommon. Routine checks prevent most of them, which is why the blood tests matter. Oestrogen slightly raises the risk of blood clots [1]. The risk is higher with smoking, long periods without moving, and some older types of oestrogen. So clinicians use estradiol, check the risk, and act on leg swelling or sudden breathlessness [1]. Testosterone can thicken the blood (a high haematocrit). The regular blood test picks this up. It is managed by changing the dose or form [1]. Spironolactone can raise potassium, and cyproterone can affect the liver. So both are checked on blood tests too [1, 2]. The long-acting testosterone injection has a rare risk in the minutes after the dose. Oil can reach the lungs, or an allergic reaction can happen. That is why the person is asked to wait at the clinic afterwards [1]. In every case, the way to prevent problems is the same. The person keeps their reviews and has blood tests when asked. They tell the prescriber or pharmacist about new medicines, smoking or symptoms.

sections.h: How to help with their medicines
body: These practical steps make the medicines side easier. For the wider picture of being an ally, see the links below.
If the person is just starting hormones, the first steps are on [Where to start with hormones](#/where-to-start).
list: Learn the name and brand of the medicine, and where the script is kept. It saves a lot of time when a pharmacy asks.
Offer to ring around pharmacies during a shortage. Use the supply page to see which products are affected.
Come to the long-acting injection appointment if asked. The [how-to guide](#/using/clinic-injection#sec-using-clinic-injection-1) explains what happens and why there is a wait afterwards.
Use the person's name and pronouns, including with pharmacy and clinic staff. Let them lead on what they share.
Do not change, hold or 'top up' doses. If something seems wrong, call the prescriber or pharmacist. In an emergency, call 000.

body: This one-page checklist is for going to the pharmacy with or for someone. It covers what to take, what to ask at the counter, and what to do if the medicine is out of stock. The same steps are in the [Easy Read guide for helpers](#/easy/helping). [Pharmacy visit checklist (PDF, 1 page)](/allies/pharmacy-visit-checklist.pdf)
This site covers the medicines. These Australian resources help you support someone through transition, at home, at school or at work:
list: [TransHub: For Allies, for carers, families, partners, friends and professionals](https://www.transhub.org.au/allies)
[Words and terms](#/terminology): plain-language words about gender and trans people, on this site
[PFLAG+ Australia: peer support for parents, carers and friends](https://pflagaustralia.org.au/)
[Transcend Australia: support for families of trans and gender diverse children](https://transcend.org.au/)
[QLife: anonymous peer support for LGBTIQ+ people and those around them, 3pm to 9pm every day, 1800 184 527](https://qlife.org.au/)
[Trans Health South Australia: directory of affirming services](https://transhealthsa.com/directory/)
